title: Indrajit's illusion
hook: the fake Sita killed before the army

segments.voice: Yesterday: sthitaprajna, the wisdom that stands still, and Rama steady in a battle that ran into the dark.

A video lands in the group chat and stomachs drop. Hours later it turns out to be fake, but by then it's been felt, believed and shared. Ravana's son has a name that means conqueror of Indra, king of the gods: Indrajit. He's one of Lanka's fiercest warriors, and his weapon isn't only arrows. It's illusion. He fights invisible, from inside the clouds. Early in the war, his arrows turn into snakes and bind Rama and Lakshmana so tight they fall as if dead. Now he tries something crueler. He rides out in his chariot in front of the whole monkey army, and beside him sits Sita.
screen: `A FAKE VIDEO, A REAL FEELING.` → `INDRAJIT: CONQUEROR OF INDRA.` → `SITA, IN HIS CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: Thin, grieving, in a dirty robe, exactly the Sita Hanuman found in the garden. Hanuman freezes. As the whole army watches, Indrajit grabs her by the hair, raises his sword, and kills her. The monkeys scatter in despair. What was the point of any of it? Hanuman runs to Rama with the news, and Rama collapses. Then Vibhishana, who knows his family, stops everything. Think, he says. Ravana would never allow Sita to be killed. It's maya: a conjured image. My nephew made a Sita out of illusion to break your heart, so you'd stop fighting while he performs a ritual that would make him unbeatable. He's right. The Sita in the chariot was never Sita. Maya is a big Sanskrit word. In everyday speech it can mean magic, trickery, illusion. In Hindu philosophy it grows much bigger: the power that makes things appear other than they are. Teachers of the Advaita tradition use a famous picture for it. In the half-dark, you see a coiled rope on the ground and jump back, heart racing: snake! Your fear is completely real. The snake never was. When the light comes, it's just rope. Advaita teachers use it to talk about the whole world and the self; other Hindu schools understand maya differently, and they'll come later on the path. Today, it's enough to see what the story sees. Indrajit's weapon was never the sword. It was the image, and the despair it caused. The way out wasn't more fighting. It was someone calmly saying: look again.
screen: `SITA IN THE CHARIOT, KILLED.` · `LOOK AGAIN, SAYS VIBHISHANA.` · `MAYA: THINGS APPEARING OTHERWISE.` · `SNAKE IN THE DARK. ROPE IN THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Remember something that crushed or frightened you and later turned out to be less than it seemed, a message read the wrong way, a look that meant nothing, and see it in the light: rope. Then hold something scaring you now, without arguing with it, and ask gently: is this a snake, or is it rope, and is there someone who could help me look again?
Indrajit's illusion. A false Sita killed in front of the army, and the calm voice that said: it's maya. Look again.
Your line: rope. The fear was real, and the snake never was. Day sixty-two, done.

howItsDone: Teachers in Advaita Vedanta often use the rope-and-snake example when explaining maya; the illusory Sita scene is told in Ramayana readings as a picture of despair built on a false image.
